name: Reverse Lunge
tierNote: Safety tier B from content.md appendix B (loaded lunge); census.json difficulty tier 1.

claims.text: The reverse lunge starts standing with the feet about hip to shoulder width apart, then one foot steps back.

quotes.text: Starting with feet hip to shoulder width, step one foot back far enough to move down into a deep lunge with the front shin approximately vertical.
With the feet about hip-width apart, slowly step backwards with the left leg.

claims.text: At the bottom the front shin is roughly vertical.

quotes.text: step one foot back far enough to move down into a deep lunge with the front shin approximately vertical.

claims.text: The trunk stays upright and the weight is shared about evenly between both feet at the bottom.

quotes.text: Keep the trunk upright and balance approximately evenly on the two feet at the bottom of the motion.

claims.text: Once the back foot lands, the back knee is lowered slowly toward the floor with the chest kept up.

quotes.text: After the left foot hits the ground push back into the right hip to slowly lower the left knee towards the floor while keeping the chest raised towards the ceiling.

claims.text: To stand up, the front foot presses into the floor while the back leg swings forward.

quotes.text: Press the right foot into the ground and think about pulling the right knee backwards while swinging the left leg forward to return to standing.

claims.text: Losing the upright trunk, the controlled descent or the balance between the feet means the load is too heavy and should be reduced.

quotes.text: Many athletes try to load lunges too heavily and lose the position in which the exercise will be most effective.
If you can't maintain a controlled descent into the bottom of the lunge, maintain an upright trunk, and maintain balance between the feet, reduce the weight.

claims.text: The descent is controlled, with a full-length step and no crashing into the bottom position.

quotes.text: Sets of 3-10 reps per leg are usually appropriate with weight that allows a full length step, smooth movement and no crashing into the bottom position.

claims.text: Leaning the trunk forward in lunges roughly doubled lower-back (erector spinae) activity in one EMG study of 12 trained women carrying 30% of body weight; that study used static, step-forward and walking lunges, not the reverse lunge.

quotes.text: Results indicate that positioning the trunk in a forward-inclined position induces greater lower lumbar erector spinae activation
(straight = 20 ± 15, inclined = 40 ± 29)
Twelve women (24 ± 3 years) were selected and performed the lunge exercise with an overload of 30% of body weight

claims.text: The reverse lunge strengthens the legs and hips and improves hip stability.

quotes.text: The reverse lunge strengthens the legs and hips and improves hip stability with the unilateral effort

claims.text: The backward lunge produced lower kneecap-joint (patellofemoral) loading than the forward lunge in 20 women without knee pain, with more forward trunk tilt.

quotes.text: Quadriceps force, PFJ reaction force, and knee flexion angle were larger in the FL movement and Up phases. PFJ loading rate was greater in the FL movement along with a lower forward trunk tilt.
The FL produced greater PFJ loading variables compared to the BL.

claims.text: The reverse lunge can be loaded with dumbbells or kettlebells held at the sides, or with a barbell.

quotes.text: The reverse lunge can be loaded in many ways, such as with a barbell in the clean rack position or overhead, dumbbells or kettlebells at the sides
Dip under the bar so that it rests behind the neck across the top of the back and the shoulder blades

claims.text: Legs can alternate each rep, or all reps can be done on one leg before switching.

quotes.text: You can alternate legs rep to rep, or complete all reps on one leg before switching to the other.

claims.text: NHS knee-pain advice: get urgent advice (111) if the knee is very painful, or locks or gives way.

quotes.text: Urgent advice: Get advice from 111 now if:
your knee is very painful
your knee locks, gives way or painfully clicks – painless clicking is normal

claims.text: Load progression: light or unloaded lunges can be done for 15-20 reps; loaded sets are usually 3-10 reps per leg at a weight that keeps a full step and smooth movement.

quotes.text: Light or unloaded lunges can be done with 15-20 reps as well if using them for work capacity or rehab.
Sets of 3-10 reps per leg are usually appropriate with weight that allows a full length step, smooth movement and no crashing into the bottom position.

claims.text: In the tempo reverse lunge (a progression), take three seconds to lower to the bottom and stand up slowly.

quotes.text: Bend both knees to 90° to lower—taking three seconds to get to the stopping point with your right knee should finish just above the floor.
Push through your left foot to stand upright slowly.

claims.text: Lower slowly and come up a little quicker; a progression is to pause at the bottom for one or two seconds, working up to about five.

quotes.text: "So you want to slowly lower yourself down and then you can go a little quicker on the way up."
One easy way Schumer likes to progress reverse lunges is to spend more time at the bottom. Start by adding just one or two seconds, then you could work up to about five seconds.

sources.title: Patellofemoral joint loading during the forward and backward lunge
Influence of Trunk Position during Three Lunge Exercises on Muscular Activation in Trained Women
Five levels of reverse lunge (Fit&Well; Amber Woolcock, certified personal trainer)
Reverse Lunge: How to Do It, Benefits, & Variations (Peloton; Rebecca Schumer, physical therapist)

plate.viewWhy: The movement is a front-to-back step in the sagittal plane; every checkpoint (shin angle c2, upright trunk c3, knee lowered to the floor c4) and the mistake (trunk pitch, c6/c8) read from the side.
plate.equipment: Two dumbbells hanging at the sides (c11), floor line.
plate.start: Standing tall, feet about hip to shoulder width apart (c1), dumbbells at the sides (c11).
plate.end: One foot stepped back, back knee lowered toward the floor (c4), front shin roughly vertical (c2), trunk upright, weight about even on both feet (c3).

checkpoints.label: Front shin vertical
checkpoints.what: At the bottom the front shin is roughly vertical.

checkpoints.label: Chest up
checkpoints.what: Trunk stays upright as the back knee lowers.

checkpoints.label: Weight even
checkpoints.what: Weight shared about evenly between both feet at the bottom.

mistake.what: Trunk pitches forward over the front thigh at the bottom (upright trunk lost).
mistake.why: Named by the anchor source as the position athletes lose when the lunge is loaded too heavily (c6); a forward-inclined trunk roughly doubled lower-back muscle activity in a lunge EMG study (c8, other lunge types).
mistake.rankNote: No source ranks lunge faults by frequency; the anchor names this fault first among the three it says heavy loading causes. Knee drifting inward is a front-view fault and is not claimed here (unsourced).

tells.text: Back knee lowers toward the floor

tempo.text: Lower slowly, rise a little quicker (c7, c16). The only number found is three seconds down in a tempo progression (c15); no source gives seconds for the rise. A bottom pause of 1–2 s, up to about 5 s, is a progression (c16), not the base tempo.

plate.variantLine: exercises.json lists Dumbbells / Barbell. The plate draws dumbbells at the sides (c11). Stance, step, shin, trunk and weight-sharing claims (c1-c5) come from a barbell source (ACE) and a load-agnostic source (Catalyst), so they hold for both.

grip.note: No reverse-lunge source covers thumb or wrist; the hold archetype's rules apply from the shared module, not from this card.

setup.step: Hold the dumbbells at your sides and stand with feet about hip to shoulder width apart.
Step one foot back, a full-length step.
Lower the back knee slowly toward the floor, chest up.
Press the front foot into the floor and bring the back leg forward to stand.
Alternate legs, or finish all reps on one side before switching.

posture.point: Front shin roughly vertical at the bottom.
Weight about even on both feet at the bottom.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Leaning the chest forward at the bottom.
handlingMistakes.fix: Go lighter until you can stay upright and controlled.
Lower slowly; use a weight that lets you move smoothly.

rows.where: Front of the thigh and the hips

rows.means: Usually means the chest is leaning forward.
rows.fix: Stay upright; go lighter if you can't.

rows.where: Knee pain that is very bad, or the knee locks or gives way

risks.risk: Too heavy a load costs the upright trunk, the controlled descent and balance.
Crashing into the bottom position instead of lowering under control.

zooms.right: Trunk upright over the hips at the bottom.
zooms.wrong: Chest pitched forward over the front thigh.
Front shin tipped far forward, not vertical.
zooms.wrongNote: The wrong drawing is the inverse of c1/c2 ; no source describes the wrong shape directly.

libraryDiff.why: Library: quads and glutes primary, hamstrings secondary, core stabilizer. Catalyst names legs and hips with a slight quad emphasis (c9), which matches; no source found that justifies a change.

loadProgression.text: Start light or unloaded; add weight only while the step stays full and the descent smooth.

anchorNote: Catalyst Athletics reverse lunge page read in full; ACE reverse lunge page also read in full.
unsourced: Knee tracking over the toes (front view) — no reverse-lunge source found.
Seconds for the rise (only "a little quicker", c16); the 3-second lowering comes from a tempo progression (c15).
Thumb and wrist for the dumbbell hold.
notes: Tempo research 2026-10-02 (LIB-3 H2, pilot A #109): c15 (Fit&Well, Woolcock) and c16 (Peloton, Schumer) added. down: 3 is from the tempo progression, not the standard lunge; the supervisor decides whether the plate uses it.
